questions.prompt: can access 1 __________ deep below the surface
questions.evidence: It hardly ever rains there, and the only year-round source of water is located tens of metres below the surface.
synonymSubstitutions: deep below the surface ↔ tens of metres below the surface
questions.distractors: ‘soil’ and ‘subsoil’ describe the material or location, but the thing accessed deep below the surface is water.

questions.prompt: was a crucial part of local inhabitants’ 2 __________ a long time ago
questions.evidence: He believes the huarango was key to the ancient people’s diet
synonymSubstitutions: local inhabitants a long time ago ↔ ancient people
questions.distractors: ‘crops’ were what later replaced huarango trees; the passage directly names diet as what the huarango was key to.

questions.prompt: helped people to survive periods of 3 __________
questions.evidence: it allowed local people to withstand years of drought when their other crops failed
synonymSubstitutions: helped people to survive ↔ allowed local people to withstand
questions.distractors: ‘failed’ describes the crops during the drought; only drought names the periods that people withstood.

questions.prompt: prevents 4 __________ of the soil
questions.evidence: Cutting down native woodland leads to erosion, as there is nothing to keep the soil in place.
synonymSubstitutions: prevents ↔ trees keep the soil in place
of the soil ↔ soil in place
questions.distractors: ‘woodland’ is what is cut down, while erosion is the damaging process that intact huarangos prevent.

questions.prompt: prevents land from becoming a 5 __________
questions.evidence: So when the huarangos go, the land turns into a desert.
synonymSubstitutions: when the huarangos go implies the trees normally prevent the change
questions.distractors: The valley is the geographical location, whereas desert is the state the land becomes without huarangos.

questions.evidence: its branches were used for charcoal for cooking and heating
synonymSubstitutions: fuel ↔ charcoal for cooking and heating
questions.distractors: Leaves and bark supplied remedies, and the trunk supplied building material; branches were the part turned into fuel.

questions.answer: leaves (and) bark [IN EITHER ORDER; BOTH REQUIRED FOR ONE MARK]
questions.answerRequirement: IN EITHER ORDER (BOTH REQUIRED FOR ONE MARK)
questions.evidence: Its leaves and bark were used for herbal remedies
synonymSubstitutions: part of tree ↔ leaves and bark
questions.distractors: Branches were used for charcoal and the trunk for houses; both leaves and bark are required for the medicine row.

questions.prompt: 8 __________ | construction
questions.evidence: its trunk was used to build houses
questions.distractors: Branches were used as fuel and leaves and bark as medicine; the trunk was the construction material.

questions.prompt: Local families have told Whaley about some traditional uses of huarango products.
questions.evidence: So, he has been working with local families to attempt to create a sustainable income from the huarangos by turning their products into foodstuffs.
synonymSubstitutions: uses of products ↔ turning their products into foodstuffs
questions.distractors: The passage states that Whaley works with local families and then describes product uses, but it never says the families told him those uses; the source of the information is absent.

questions.prompt: Farmer Alberto Benevides is now making a good profit from growing huarangos.
questions.evidence: His farm is relatively small and doesn’t yet provide him with enough to live on, but he hopes this will change.
synonymSubstitutions: now making a good profit contradicts doesn’t yet provide enough to live on
questions.distractors: Benevides does sell syrup and flour, but the explicit statement that the farm does not yet support him contradicts a good current profit.

questions.prompt: Whaley needs the co-operation of farmers to help preserve the area’s wildlife.
questions.evidence: In the hope of counteracting this, he’s persuading farmers to let him plant forest corridors on their land.
synonymSubstitutions: needs the co-operation of farmers ↔ persuading farmers to let him
preserve wildlife ↔ corridors allow movement of mammals, birds and pollen
questions.distractors: The cooperation is not merely implied by general community support: the passage explicitly says forest corridors must be planted on farmers’ land to counter habitat fragmentation.

questions.prompt: For Whaley’s project to succeed, it needs to be extended over a very large area.
questions.evidence: It’s not like a rainforest that needs to have this huge expanse. Life has always been confined to corridors and islands here. If you just have a few trees left, the population can grow up quickly because it’s used to exploiting water when it arrives.
synonymSubstitutions: needs to be extended contradicts a few trees left can support quick growth
questions.distractors: Although Whaley hopes the model can later be rolled out elsewhere, he explicitly says this desert habitat does not require a huge expanse.

questions.prompt: Whaley has plans to go to Africa to set up a similar project.
questions.evidence: He sees his project as a model that has the potential to be rolled out across other arid areas around the world. ‘If we can do it here, in the most fragile system on Earth, then that’s a real message of hope for lots of places, including Africa
synonymSubstitutions: similar project ↔ model with potential to be rolled out
questions.distractors: Africa is mentioned only as a place that could receive a message of hope; no travel plan or intention by Whaley to establish a project there is stated.

questions.prompt: La Gomera is the most mountainous of all the Canary Islands.
questions.evidence: This small volcanic island is mountainous, with steep rocky slopes and deep, wooded ravines, rising to 1,487 metres at its highest peak.
questions.distractors: No comparison with every other Canary Island is given. TRUE adds an unsupported superlative; FALSE would require proof that another island is more mountainous.

questions.prompt: Silbo is only appropriate for short and simple messages.
questions.evidence: ‘In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands, but any Spanish sentence could be whistled.’
synonymSubstitutions: short and simple messages ↔ short commands
only appropriate ↔ any Spanish sentence could be whistled
questions.distractors: ‘Short commands’ tempts TRUE, but ‘any Spanish sentence’ directly contradicts ‘only’; the issue is explicit, so NOT GIVEN is excluded.

questions.prompt: In the brain-activity study, silbadores and non-whistlers produced different results.
questions.evidence: The researchers found that other key regions in the brain’s frontal lobe also responded to the whistles, including those activated in response to sign language among deaf people. When the experiments were repeated with non-whistlers, however, activation was observed in all areas of the brain.
synonymSubstitutions: different results ↔ key regions / all areas
questions.distractors: ‘However’ marks the explicit contrast. FALSE denies it, and NOT GIVEN ignores the reported results.

questions.prompt: The Spanish introduced Silbo to the islands in the 15th century.
questions.evidence: indigenous Canary Islanders, who were of North African origin, already had a whistled language when Spain conquered the volcanic islands in the 15th century
questions.distractors: The date and Spain tempt TRUE, but ‘already had’ shows the language predated conquest; the chronology excludes NOT GIVEN.

questions.prompt: There is precise data available regarding all of the whistle languages in existence today.
questions.evidence: There are thought to be as many as 70 whistled languages still in use, though only 12 have been described and studied scientifically.
synonymSubstitutions: in existence today ↔ still in use
precise data regarding all ↔ only 12 studied scientifically
questions.distractors: ‘As many as 70’ is an estimate and only 12 are studied, contradicting precise data for all; this is stated, so NOT GIVEN is excluded.

questions.prompt: The children of Gomera now learn Silbo.
questions.evidence: Since 1999, Silbo Gomero has been taught in all of the island’s elementary schools.
synonymSubstitutions: children of Gomera ↔ island’s elementary schools
now learn ↔ has been taught since 1999
questions.distractors: The school programme directly supports the statement; FALSE contradicts it and NOT GIVEN overlooks it.

questions.prompt: high- and low-frequency tones represent different sounds in Spanish 20 __________
questions.evidence: Silbo is a substitute for Spanish, with individual words recoded into whistles which have high- and low-frequency tones.
synonymSubstitutions: represent different sounds ↔ recoded into whistles
questions.distractors: Whistles are the recoded form and tones are frequencies; the plural item represented is words.

questions.prompt: pitch of whistle is controlled using silbador’s 21 __________
questions.evidence: A whistler – or silbador – puts a finger in his or her mouth to increase the whistle’s pitch
questions.distractors: Mouth is the location, but finger is the instrument; hand controls direction in the next note.

questions.prompt: 22 __________ is changed with a cupped hand
questions.evidence: the other hand can be cupped to adjust the direction of the sound
synonymSubstitutions: with a cupped hand ↔ hand can be cupped
questions.distractors: Pitch is changed with a finger; sound is general, while direction is the precise property adjusted.

questions.prompt: in everyday use for the transmission of brief 23 __________
questions.evidence: ‘In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands, but any Spanish sentence could be whistled.’
questions.distractors: Sentence describes wider capability; routine use is specifically for commands. Information is too broad.

questions.prompt: can relay essential information quickly, e.g. to inform people about 24 __________
questions.evidence: Silbo has proved particularly useful when fires have occurred on the island and rapid communication across large areas has been vital.
questions.distractors: Areas is the reach and island the location; fires are the emergency communicated about.

questions.prompt: future under threat because of new 25 __________
questions.evidence: But with modern communication technology now widely available, researchers say whistled languages like Silbo are threatened with extinction.
synonymSubstitutions: future under threat ↔ threatened with extinction
questions.distractors: Communication modifies technology; extinction is the outcome, not the cause.

questions.prompt: Canaries’ authorities hoping to receive a UNESCO 26 __________ to help preserve it
questions.evidence: ‘The local authorities are trying to get an award from the organisation to declare [Silbo Gomero] as something that should be preserved for humanity,’ Carreiras adds.
synonymSubstitutions: hoping to receive ↔ trying to get
questions.distractors: Assistance is a general request, but the quotation and article ‘a’ identify award; organisation refers to UNESCO itself.

questions.prompt: Many big businesses today are prepared to harm people and the environment in order to make money, and they appear to have no __________.
questions.evidence: businesses are not charities but profit-making companies

distractors.C: Rare species are not identified here.

synonymSubstitutions: no moral standards ↔ not charities / maximize profits

questions.prompt: Lack of __________ by governments
questions.evidence: the reverse is likely to be true if government regulation is ineffective

distractors.C: Rare species are not government action.

questions.prompt: lack of public __________
questions.evidence: When government regulation is effective, and when the public is environmentally aware, environmentally clean big businesses may out-compete dirty ones, but the reverse is likely to be true if government regulation is ineffective and if the public doesn't care.

distractors.A: Funding is not the named public condition.
distractors.C: Rare species are not a public quality.
distractors.D: The public is not said to lack moral standards.

questions.prompt: environmental problems such as __________
questions.evidence: fishermen in an unmanaged fishery without quotas

distractors.A: Funding is not an environmental problem.

questions.prompt: the destruction of __________
questions.evidence: international logging companies with short-term leases on tropical rainforest land

distractors.C: Rare species are not explicitly the target.

synonymSubstitutions: destruction of trees ↔ logging rainforest land

questions.prompt: The main idea of the third paragraph is that environmental damage

options.A: requires political action if it is to be stopped.
options.B: is the result of ignorance on the part of the public.
options.C: could be prevented by the action of ordinary people.
options.D: can only be stopped by educating business leaders.

questions.evidence: it is the public, either directly or through its politicians, that has the power to make such destructive policies unprofitable and illegal

distractors.A: Politics is only one route; direct public action is also named.
distractors.B: Public ignorance is not given as the cause.
distractors.D: Educating business leaders is not mentioned.

questions.prompt: In the fourth paragraph, the writer describes ways in which the public can

options.A: reduce their own individual impact on the environment.
options.B: learn more about the impact of business on the environment.
options.C: raise awareness of the effects of specific environmental disasters.
options.D: influence the environmental policies of businesses and governments.

questions.evidence: The public may also make their opinion felt by preferring to buy sustainably harvested products; by making employees of companies with poor track records feel ashamed of their company and complain to their own management; by preferring their governments to award valuable contracts to businesses with a good environmental track record; and by pressing their governments to pass and enforce laws and regulations requiring good environmental practices.

distractors.A: The actions target companies and government, not only personal impact.
distractors.B: The paragraph recommends action, not learning.
distractors.C: Exxon Valdez illustrates suing, not awareness raising.

synonymSubstitutions: influence policies ↔ buying choices / contracts / pressing governments

questions.prompt: What pressure was exerted by big business in the case of the disease BSE?

options.A: Meat packers stopped supplying hamburgers to fast-food chains.
options.B: A fast-food company forced their meat suppliers to follow the law.
options.C: Meat packers persuaded the government to reduce their expenses.
options.D: A fast-food company encouraged the government to introduce legislation.

questions.evidence: However, when a major fast-food company then made the same demands after customer purchases of its hamburgers plummeted, the meat industry complied within weeks.

distractors.A: Packers did not stop supplying hamburgers.
distractors.C: They did not obtain reduced expenses.
distractors.D: Government rules existed before the company demand.

questions.prompt: The public should be prepared to fund good environmental practices.
questions.evidence: the public must accept the necessity for higher prices for products to cover the added costs, if any, of sound environmental practices

distractors.NOT GIVEN: The writer directly states the claim.

synonymSubstitutions: fund ↔ accept higher prices to cover costs

questions.prompt: There is a contrast between the moral principles of different businesses.
questions.evidence: businesses should act in accordance with moral principles even if this leads to a reduction in their profits

distractors.YES: No comparison between different businesses is made.
distractors.NO: The writer does not say their principles are the same.

questions.prompt: It is important to make a clear distinction between acceptable and unacceptable behaviour.
questions.evidence: My conclusion is not a moralistic one about who is right or wrong, admirable or selfish, a good guy or a bad guy.

distractors.YES: The writer explicitly rejects a moralistic division.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The writer states his position directly.

synonymSubstitutions: distinction ↔ right or wrong / good guy or bad guy

questions.prompt: The public have successfully influenced businesses in the past.
questions.evidence: In the past, businesses have changed when the public came to expect and require different behavior

distractors.NO: Past public-caused change is explicitly stated.

synonymSubstitutions: in the past ↔ In the past

questions.prompt: In the future, businesses will show more concern for the environment.
questions.evidence: I predict that in the future, just as in the past, changes in public attitudes will be essential for changes in businesses' environmental practices.

distractors.YES: A necessary condition is predicted, not that more concern will occur.
distractors.NO: Less concern is not predicted either.

questions.prompt: What would be the best subheading for this passage?

options.A: Will the world survive the threat caused by big businesses?
options.B: How can big businesses be encouraged to be less driven by profit?
options.C: What environmental dangers are caused by the greed of businesses?
options.D: Are big businesses to blame for the damage they cause the environment?

questions.evidence: Our blaming of businesses also ignores the ultimate responsibility of the public for creating the conditions that let a business profit through destructive environmental policies.
questions.evidenceLocation: Paragraphs C and G; physical pages 90–91.

distractors.A: Survival of the world is not the focus.
distractors.B: The passage accepts the profit duty and focuses on incentives and responsibility.
distractors.C: Environmental dangers are examples, not the central argument.
